description: We are building a physical, tactile Earth map that translates NASA satellite data into touchable textures, vibration feedback, and Braille legends for deafblind users. Looking for teammates interested in accessibility, physical prototyping, hardware/design, and Earth science. I am young student of Grade 9 so looking forward my team mates.
summary:
This project addresses data inaccessibility in NASA and climate datasets, enabling blind and visually impaired individuals to connect with our Earth and universe. I developed an interactive web application that converts climate datasets into piano sonification, mapping lower values to low-frequency piano notes and rising temperatures and carbon dioxide  levels to increasing frequencies .
The app features dropdown menus for parameters and start years, adjustable time slots , and volume controls . Users can play data from 1958 onwards or from a selected year forward, keeping frequency data separate.
To solve navigation barriers, the webpage features a prominent, full-width audio button labeled "LISTEN TO SCREEN GUIDE." When activated, it reads aloud where every button, dropdown, slider, and graph is located on the screen, allowing blind users to effortlessly explore the application. This project is vital because it democratizes science, ensuring visually impaired learners can independently experience climate data and engage with our changing world.
details:
This project helps blind and visually impaired individuals connect with our Earth and universe by converting NASA and global climate datasets into piano sonification.

How it works: Users begin by selecting one of two parameters: temperature anomaly or carbon dioxide level. Next, they select a start year or choose to play from the beginning (1958 onwards). Users can also customize their experience by adjusting the volume (1% to 100%) and setting a specific time slot duration (20 to 30 seconds) to listen to the piano notes for that timeframe. When playback starts, the app plays each year's data point on the piano without merging the frequency channels—mapping lower values to low piano notes and increasing values to higher notes. Additionally, the webpage features two comparison graphs for carbon dioxide and temperature that visually demonstrate how rising carbon dioxide drives rising temperatures.

The primary benefit is that it removes visual barriers, making scientific exploration accessible, inclusive, and engaging for non-sighted learners. The intended impact is to empower visually impaired and low-vision individuals to independently explore data, fostering a globally inclusive scientific community.

To build this project, we used HTML for coding the interactive web application and Google Slides for initial planning and design.

The project is creative because, instead of traditional small buttons, it features prominent, full-width action buttons designed for easy physical and screen-reader navigation. Crucially, it includes an audio screen guide button that vocally narrates the layout and location of every control.

When developing this, our team considered accessibility as the core principle, ensuring complex climate data is fully experienceable through clear audio feedback. We factored in user-friendly layout design by keeping interface elements uncluttered, large, and fully navigable for users relying on assistive technology.
